title: The history of the telephone
tagline: From a voice on a string to calls as packets of light: 150 years of talking at a distance.
intro: People dreamed of sending a voice along a wire long before anyone managed it. In the 1870s several inventors raced to do it, and Alexander Graham Bell won the patent. Then came the harder part: loud microphones, exchanges to connect everyone, switches that counted your dial pulses, cables under oceans, and finally digital voices, fibre and the internet. India joined early, in 1882, and in the 1980s and 90s built its own exchanges and filled its streets with yellow STD booths.

eras.name: A voice down a wire
eras.summary: Scientists and tinkerers show that sound can travel along a string or a wire, and several inventors try to send speech by electricity.

eras.name: The telephone is born
eras.summary: Bell patents the telephone, and carbon microphones make calls loud enough to be useful.

eras.name: Operators and switchboards
eras.summary: Exchanges connect whole towns, and operators, mostly women, join calls by hand with plugs and cords.

eras.name: Switches that count
eras.summary: Strowger's stepping switch, the rotary dial, crossbar grids and touch-tone let callers connect themselves.

eras.name: Across continents and oceans
eras.summary: Amplifiers, radio, undersea cables and satellites stretch calls across continents and oceans.

eras.name: India dials in
eras.summary: From Calcutta's 93 subscribers to STD dialling, C-DOT's own exchanges and a booth on every corner.

eras.name: Digital, fibre and the internet
eras.summary: Voices become numbers, exchanges become computers, and calls travel as packets over fibre.

events.title: Sound travels down a string
events.text: The English scientist Robert Hooke described how sound could be carried far along a tight wire or string, much further than through the air. It is the idea behind the tin-can telephone that children still make.
events.why: Long before electricity, people knew a solid line could carry a voice.

events.title: A 'Telephon' plays music by wire
events.text: The German teacher Philipp Reis showed a device he called the Telephon. It sent musical tones, and by some accounts a few words, down a wire. Historians still argue about how well it carried speech.
events.why: It gave the telephone its name, 15 years before Bell's patent.

events.title: Meucci's 'telettrofono'
events.text: The Italian inventor Antonio Meucci had been working on a talking telegraph, his telettrofono, for years. Too poor to pay for a full patent, he filed a cheaper caveat in 1871 and let it lapse in 1874. In 2002 the US House of Representatives passed a resolution saying his work in the invention of the telephone should be acknowledged. Who deserves the most credit is still debated.
events.why: The telephone had several parents, and not all of them got the credit.

events.title: Bell patents the telephone
events.text: Bell's lawyer filed his patent application on 14 February 1876, the same day Elisha Gray filed a caveat for a similar idea. US patent 174,465 was granted on 7 March. Three days later Bell spoke the first words over his liquid transmitter: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.'
events.why: It was one of the most valuable patents ever, and the start of the Bell telephone companies.

events.title: Carbon makes the voice loud
events.text: Early telephones were faint. Thomas Edison filed a patent in 1877 for a transmitter that used carbon, whose resistance changes when pressed. David Edward Hughes showed a carbon 'microphone' in London in 1878, and many historians credit him with the idea. Carbon microphones were used in telephones for about a hundred years.
events.why: The carbon microphone let a voice control a battery's current, making calls loud enough to be practical.

events.title: The first telephone exchange
events.text: George Coy opened the first commercial telephone exchange, with 21 subscribers. His switchboard was built from carriage bolts and wire from ladies' bustles, and could connect two conversations at a time.
events.why: For the first time you could call anyone on the exchange, not just one other phone.

events.title: Emma Nutt, the first woman operator
events.text: Early operators were teenage boys, who were often rude to callers. Emma Nutt was hired as the first woman operator, and her sister Stella started a few hours later. Within a few years, switchboards everywhere were run by women.
events.why: Operating the switchboard became one of the first big jobs open to women.

events.title: India's first telephone exchanges
events.text: The Oriental Telephone Company opened exchanges in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. The Central Exchange in Calcutta had 93 subscribers.
events.why: The telephone reached India just six years after Bell's patent.

events.title: A switch with no operator
events.text: Almon Strowger, an undertaker, patented an automatic stepping switch. The story goes that he believed a local operator was sending his customers' calls to a rival. In his switch, electrical pulses from the caller move a wiper up and round to the right line.
events.why: It began the end of manual switchboards: the exchange could now count the number itself.

events.title: The first automatic exchange
events.text: The first commercial automatic exchange, using Strowger's switch, opened in La Porte. Early callers pressed buttons to send the pulses; the finger-wheel rotary dial followed over the next years.
events.why: A small town showed that a phone network could run without operators.

events.title: The rotary dial takes shape
events.text: Engineers working with Strowger's company developed the rotary dial, which breaks the line current once for each step as a spring turns it back. By about 1907 the familiar finger-wheel dial with a finger stop had arrived.
events.why: The rotary dial made the caller the operator, one pulse at a time.

events.title: India's first automatic exchange
events.text: The summer capital of British India got the country's first automatic exchange, with a capacity of 700 lines and about 400 working connections.
events.why: Automatic switching arrived in India only two decades after La Porte.

events.title: A call across a continent
events.who: Alexander Graham Bell and Thomas Watson
events.text: Bell, in New York, spoke to his old assistant Watson in San Francisco, about 5,500 km away. Vacuum-tube amplifiers along the line kept the voice loud enough to hear.
events.why: Amplifiers meant distance no longer killed the voice.

events.title: Crossbar switches
events.text: Crossbar switches store the dialled number first, then close a single crosspoint in a grid of horizontal and vertical bars. Sweden used Betulander's design from 1926; the US No. 1 crossbar entered service in 1938.
events.why: Crossbar was faster and more reliable than step-by-step, and ran many networks until the digital age.

events.title: Talking across the Atlantic by radio
events.who: AT&T and the British General Post Office
events.text: The first commercial telephone service between North America and Europe opened, carried by radio. A three-minute call cost about 75 US dollars at the time.
events.why: For the first time, voices crossed an ocean the same day, not weeks later by ship.

events.title: Voices as numbers
events.text: The British engineer Alec Reeves, working for an ITT company in France, invented pulse-code modulation: measuring a sound wave thousands of times a second and sending each measurement as a number. It was too early for the electronics of the day.
events.why: Every digital phone call, and much of today's audio, still uses his idea.

events.title: TAT-1: the first transatlantic telephone cable
events.who: British Post Office, AT&T and Canada
events.text: TAT-1 carried 35 telephone calls at once across the Atlantic, with 51 amplifiers, called repeaters, sealed along the sea bed. In its first 24 hours it carried 588 calls between London and the US.
events.why: Undersea cables made international calls clear and common; their fibre successors carry the internet today.

events.title: India's first STD call
events.text: Subscriber trunk dialling, STD, let callers dial another city themselves instead of booking a 'trunk call' through an operator. India's first STD route linked Lucknow and Kanpur.
events.why: It was the first step from waiting hours for a trunk call to dialling any city at once.

events.title: Telstar relays calls through space
events.who: AT&T, Bell Labs, NASA and partners
events.text: The Telstar 1 satellite relayed the first live television pictures and telephone calls across the Atlantic. Later satellites were parked in geostationary orbit, 35,786 km up, which adds about a quarter of a second each way.
events.why: Satellites connected places cables could not reach, but their delay made chatting awkward.

events.title: Touch-tone
events.text: The Bell System offered push-button 'Touch-Tone' phones to the public. Each key sends two tones at once, one for its row and one for its column. The same tones still work when a helpline says 'press 1'.
events.why: Dialling became faster, and the keypad became a way to talk to machines.

events.title: A computer runs the exchange
events.text: The No. 1 Electronic Switching System was the first big exchange controlled by a stored program, like a computer. New services could be added by changing software instead of rewiring.
events.why: Exchanges became computers, which made features like call waiting and call forwarding possible.

events.title: The first fully digital exchanges
events.text: The E10 system, developed from research at Lannion, became the first fully digital local exchange to serve customers. Voices were switched as streams of numbers in time slots.
events.why: Digital switching made exchanges smaller, cheaper and far more reliable.

events.title: C-DOT: India builds its own exchanges
events.who: Sam Pitroda and the Government of India
events.text: The Centre for Development of Telematics was set up to design digital exchanges for Indian conditions: small, rugged rural exchanges (RAX) that could work in heat and dust without air conditioning, and larger ones for cities. Indian firms were licensed to make them.
events.why: It put automatic telephones within reach of small towns and villages across India.

events.title: The STD/ISD/PCO booth revolution
events.who: Department of Telecommunications and booth owners
events.text: Yellow STD/ISD/PCO booths spread to street corners, shops and villages, often run by young entrepreneurs and people with disabilities. For the first time, millions of people without a home phone could dial any city, or any country, themselves. Mobile phones made them rare by the 2010s.
events.why: Public phones brought long-distance calling to ordinary people and created many small businesses.

events.title: Light under the Atlantic
events.who: AT&T, France Télécom and British Telecom
events.text: TAT-8, the first transatlantic fibre-optic cable, carried calls as flashes of light, with about 40,000 circuits by most accounts. Fibre soon replaced copper and satellites on the world's busiest routes.
events.why: Glass fibre gave calls, and then the internet, almost unlimited room.

events.title: Calls over the internet
events.text: VocalTec released InternetPhone, one of the first programs to carry voice calls over the internet (VoIP). Services like Skype (2003) and today's fibre home phones grew from the same idea.
events.why: Your voice became data, sharing the same network as web pages and videos.

events.title: One number for emergencies: 112
events.text: India launched the Emergency Response Support System with a single emergency number, 112, for police, fire, ambulance and more, as used across Europe.
events.why: One easy number, from any phone, can save lives.

events.title: Landlines halve
events.text: Fixed telephone lines fell from 20 per 100 people in 2005 to 11 per 100 in 2023, about 861 million lines, as mobiles took over. Many remaining lines now run over fibre rather than copper.
events.why: The landline is fading, but the ideas inside it, from dialling to digital voice, live on in every mobile call.

people.note: Patented a carbon transmitter that made telephone calls loud and clear.

series.title: Telephones in India before mobiles
series.caption: India's telephone count grew slowly for decades, then faster once STD and home-built exchanges arrived.

facts: A 0 on a rotary dial sends ten pulses and takes a full second to dial.
Calcutta's first telephone exchange, in 1882, had just 93 subscribers.
TAT-1, the first transatlantic telephone cable, carried 588 calls between London and the US in its first 24 hours.
The touch-tone keypad has a secret fourth column, A, B, C and D, which home phones almost never showed.
Almon Strowger, who automated the telephone exchange, was an undertaker.
